name: Raymond Fletcher
presenting_complaint: Two episodes of vomiting fresh red blood, now dizzy and hypotensive

conditions: Alcohol-related chronic liver disease with known oesophageal varices
medications: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily (self-directed for knee pain)
medical_history.social: Drinks approximately 8 standard drinks daily for 25 years. Ex-smoker. Lives with partner.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 61-year-old man is brought to ED after two episodes of vomiting fresh red blood at home, now feeling faint. He has known alcohol-related chronic liver disease with previously documented oesophageal varices and has been taking naproxen for knee pain. He looks pale, clammy and anxious. Obs: BP 86/52, HR 122, RR 24, SpO2 96% on room air, GCS 15.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Characterise the bleed: volume and colour of haematemesis (fresh red vs coffee-ground), number of episodes, any melaena or fresh PR bleeding, timing
Risk factors for variceal bleed: chronic liver disease, alcohol history, known oesophageal varices, previous variceal bleeds/banding
Risk factors for peptic ulcer bleed: NSAID use (naproxen), prior dyspepsia/ulcer, H. pylori, steroids
Anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and any bleeding tendency; document allergies and full medication list
Symptoms of hypovolaemia/decompensation: dizziness, syncope, chest pain; screen for encephalopathy and ascites
objective: A-to-E assessment with quantified haemodynamic status: this patient is shocked (BP 86/52, HR 122) — recognise Class III haemorrhagic shock
Insert TWO large-bore (14-16G) IV cannulas and take bloods at cannulation
Bloods: FBC, UEC (urea disproportionately raised in upper GI bleed), LFT, coagulation profile/INR, VBG with lactate, and GROUP AND CROSSMATCH (not just group and hold given active bleeding)
Stigmata of chronic liver disease: jaundice, spider naevi, ascites, asterixis, splenomegaly; PR exam for melaena
Insert urinary catheter for hourly output; calculate Glasgow-Blatchford score to gauge severity
assessment: Acute upper GI haemorrhage with haemorrhagic shock
Suspected variceal bleed given known oesophageal varices and chronic liver disease — treat down the variceal pathway
Peptic ulcer bleed a key differential given NSAID (naproxen) use; both may coexist
plan: Two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch, and ACTIVATE THE MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL given active bleeding with haemodynamic instability (FIRST action)
Resuscitate: balanced crystalloid while blood is prepared; nil by mouth; urinary catheter; continuous monitoring

Transfuse red cells to a RESTRICTIVE target of Hb approximately 70 g/L (aim 70-90 g/L; higher ~80 g/L if significant cardiac disease) unless exsanguinating — avoid over-transfusion which worsens variceal bleeding
Correct coagulopathy per Lifeblood/haematology advice; stop naproxen and perindopril; withhold/reverse any anticoagulants
VARICEAL PATHWAY: commence terlipressin 2 mg IV (or octreotide infusion) AND prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone 1 g IV) — antibiotics improve survival in cirrhotic GI bleeds
High-dose IV proton pump inhibitor (e.g. pantoprazole 80 mg IV bolus then infusion) to cover peptic ulcer aetiology
Urgent referral to gastroenterology for endoscopy within 24 hours (earlier if unstable) for band ligation/injection; consider ICU/HDU admission
Escalate early to senior/ED consultant and consider balloon tamponade (Sengstaken) as a bridge if uncontrolled variceal haemorrhage

critical_errors: Treating this as a simple peptic ulcer bleed and omitting the variceal pathway (terlipressin/octreotide PLUS prophylactic antibiotics) despite known varices and chronic liver disease
Failing to activate massive transfusion / crossmatch and site two large-bore cannulas in a shocked, actively bleeding patient
Over-transfusing to a liberal Hb target instead of a restrictive target (~70 g/L), which raises portal pressure and worsens variceal bleeding
must_not_miss: Variceal haemorrhage requiring terlipressin/octreotide + antibiotics + urgent endoscopy
Haemorrhagic shock requiring massive transfusion activation and restrictive transfusion strategy
Ongoing nephrotoxic/precipitant drugs (naproxen, perindopril, anticoagulants) stopped or reversed
